meta.title: German C2 — Vocabulary
meta.subtitle: 3000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: German → English (see the German, recall the meaning) and English → German (see an English meaning, recall the German). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 3000 words for reading German at C2, the level at which a learner reads virtually everything with ease and catches what is implied as well as what is said. There is no Goethe C2 word list, and that is the exam board's own position rather than something missing here. The published Wortlisten stop at B1, and the Goethe-Institut gives its reason in the C1 Prüfungsziele/Testbeschreibung, section 4.4: „Wortschatz- und Grammatikinventare zum Goethe-Zertifikat C1 gibt es aus folgenden Gründen nicht: Auf dieser Stufe läßt sich keine verbindliche Eingrenzung des Wortschatzes vornehmen, da authentische Texte verwendet werden.“ — no binding delimitation of the vocabulary can be made at that level, because the exam uses authentic texts; the C2 brochure names no inventory either. So this deck does not claim to be that list. It is the vocabulary a reader who already has A1, A2, B1, B2 and C1 will actually meet in written German: the most frequent words beyond those in a corpus of one million sentences of German news (the Leipzig Corpora Collection's deu_news_2024, 17.6 million words), which is the register the reading passages at this level are drawn from. Only the ranking is taken from that corpus — not one of its sentences appears in this deck. Proper names, inflected forms, regional and place-derived words, and words spelt the same in English are left out. So are compounds that can simply be read off their parts (Bushaltestelle, Wahlergebnis), on the Institut's own reasoning in the same passage: a candidate at this level is expected to decode those rather than to have learnt them. The cards are ordered by roughly how often a word is used, so the ones you meet most often come first. The measure is one scale for every deck here: how often the word turns up per million words of film and television dialogue, plus how often it turns up per million words of newspaper German. Neither corpus does the job alone — the spoken one barely knows the vocabulary of the upper levels, and the written one flattens the everyday words the lower ones are about — so the two are added, and the spoken register decides among the very common words while the written register decides among the rest. The spoken list is written without capitals, so it cannot tell Würde from würde; where a word is spelled like another that way, its share of that list is the share the written corpus gives it. The three levels are cut on that same scale, so they are frequency bands rather than three separate lists: what separates this one from the next is where a word falls on it, and even the rarest word here turns up 8 times in the newspaper corpus. Every noun carries its article, so the gender is learnt with the word (1899 of them), and the article is coloured by gender: der blue, die red, das green. Its plural sits directly beneath it (1693 of them). Where a noun names a person its feminine is given too (184), so that beside der Verfasser stands die Verfasserin. Each of the 515 verbs carries its full paradigm: the infinitive, the past participle and the auxiliary it takes, then the present, the Präteritum, the Perfekt and the imperative, each in all six persons from ich to sie/Sie. The Perfekt is the point — it is how a German speaker talks about the past, and whether a verb takes haben or sein has to be learnt with the verb. A separable verb is shown as it is really said, ich fahre ab rather than ich abfahre. The polite imperative is given as well as the du and ihr forms: seien Sie ruhig, fahren Sie ab. Adjectives carry their comparative and superlative (323 of them), since German umlauts them unpredictably — groß, größer, am größten. Real example sentences come with 1830 of the 3000 words, three apiece for 1020 of them and one or two for the rest; the sentence corpus has nothing at all for the other 1170, which are kept because the words are chosen from written German and the sentence corpus is a corpus of everyday speech, which simply has less to say about them, chosen where possible to show three different inflected forms rather than the same one three times, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside it. Word selection: the Leipzig Corpora Collection, deu_news_2024 (wortschatz-leipzig.de), used for word frequencies only. Meanings, genders, plurals, feminines and conjugations: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0) together with the Leipzig Corpora Collection, deu_news_2024 (wortschatz-leipzig.de). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
